articles.text: engineering guide · 30 october 2026 · web security how to render markdown citation links without introducing xss a technical article needs hyperlinks to repositories, standards and documentation. but a user-supplied markdown link can contain unexpected schemes, html-like labels and credentials embedded in a url. we extended the browser-only 24gotop draft lab to support a deliberately small link syntax and tested the failure cases first. by 24gotop engineering · 30 october 2026 · merged pr #78 · regression tests scope: this is a limited author-side preview, not a general-purpose commonmark implementation or a public publishing backend. it does not support embedded images, rich html or arbitrary url schemes. no user-generated content is sent to the server. what should a citation link accept? our initial preview treated all markdown syntax as plain text, an intentional safety-first choice documented in the original dom preview design . later, authors needed references in the text they were writing. we chose a narrow [label](https://example.org/path) syntax instead of permitting arbitrary html. the preview recognizes a bounded link label and url. the target must be an actual http or https url with a hostname, without embedded usernames or passwords. parentheses, backslashes, whitespace and nested markdown are excluded from the supported form. unsupported syntax remains visible as text; the parser does not attempt to repair it into a risky link. validate the url before creating an anchor the public renderer includes a dedicated url gate. it uses the platform url parser and then checks the exact protocol, hostname and credential fields: export function safecitationurl(raw) { if (typeof raw !== 'string' || raw.length > 1500) return null; try { const url = new url(raw); return ['https:', 'http:'].includes(url.protocol) && url.hostname && !url.username && !url.password && url.href.length <= 2048 ? url.href : null; } catch { return null; } } do not rely only on a string prefix such as startswith('http') . scheme-like strings and unusual url syntax are easy to misread. the normalized url object gives you explicit components to check. the restrictive markdown tokenizer further rules out input shapes we have not chosen to support. build dom nodes, never concatenate untrusted html for every accepted link, the editor creates a fixed a element, sets its visible label with textcontent and its validated destination with setattribute . the renderer does not interpolate the raw label into an html string or assign user content to innerhtml . const link = document.createelement('a'); link.textcontent = label; link.setattribute('href', safeurl); link.setattribute('rel', 'noopener noreferrer ugc'); link.setattribute('target', '_blank'); link.setattribute('referrerpolicy', 'no-referrer'); those attributes address different concerns. noopener prevents a new page from controlling its opener; noreferrer and the referrer policy limit referral information; ugc describes the link as user-generated. none of these makes a malicious external website trustworthy. a reader still chooses whether to follow it. the page's surrounding text is added as text nodes. inline code and fenced code are treated separately, so an author can discuss a malicious url or show a code sample containing markdown syntax without accidentally creating a link in the preview. adversarial test cases worth keeping our tests exercise meaningful security cases: a markdown label resembling an image with an event handler; a javascript: destination; credential-bearing https://user:password@host urls; and link-looking syntax inside a code fence. when the parser rejects a link, the text stays noninteractive, and no unsafe anchor is created. the companion formatting tests verify that the editor's link button wraps a selected single-line label, highlights a placeholder https destination for editing, and rejects oversized or multiline selections without losing the original article body. this is a testable design contract, not an assertion that every possible markdown or url edge case is covered. in a hosted publishing platform, additional controls would include strict content security policy, vetted rendering libraries, moderation decisions, safe external redirects where needed and real-browser adversarial testing. why this matters for technical seo and ai citations original technical documentation should make sources inspectable. a real hyperlink lets a human or browsing assistant follow the cited specification, github pr or regression test. a visible source title without a usable link is harder to independently verify, but a link is valuable only if it is safely represented and not an implied endorsement. google's official ai-search guidance emphasizes crawlable, useful visible content and ordinary seo fundamentals. it does not promise ai-feature placement merely because a page has links, special ai markup or an optional text index. we use explicit links for reader utility and provenance, not to simulate authority or engineer artificial backlinks. how to reproduce the implementation review public pr #78 for the dom rendering and url-validation changes. clone the repository , run npm run check and npm test on node.js 22+, then inspect the exact safe/unsafe test cases. try the browser-only draft lab : highlight some technical text, choose link , replace the destination with a real https documentation url, and inspect the preview. compare the old text-only preview rationale with the new allowed syntax. a new feature should extend a reviewed trust boundary deliberately, not accidentally. bottom line: treat markdown links as untrusted input, constrain what you parse, validate normalized urls, create only fixed dom nodes and test rejected syntax as seriously as successful links. that approach is useful beyond 24gotop—to documentation editors, issue trackers and developer knowledge tools. primary evidence: pr #78 , live source , security tests and independent https delivery check . the community publishing backend remains pre-launch. read more engineering guides ↗

engineering guide · 30 october 2026 · ci/cd & search how to verify a github pages deployment—not just a green ci badge a successful pull request confirms the repository changed. a green deployment action confirms a deployment workflow completed. neither proves a reader can fetch the correct html and javascript from your canonical domain. we learned this during a real 24gotop release and turned the failure into a reproducible deployment check. by 24gotop engineering · 30 october 2026 · https verification pr #79 · race fix pr #82 what was verified: the public static pages and assets were fetched over https from https://24go.top by github-hosted runners. no measurement here proves constant uptime, google indexing, production accounts, or a live user publishing api. this site is still pre-launch. the three different questions you must answer is the code correct? unit tests, linting, build checks and source review can show the intended content and behavior under test conditions. did deployment finish? the official github pages workflow reports whether uploading and publishing the static artifact succeeded. is the actual site serving the update? an independent request must fetch the canonical https url, follow safe redirects and inspect the resulting html/js files for a release-specific, truthful marker. these are separate observations. a deployment can finish before a cdn edge serves new content; a test can also run before the deployment finishes. reporting “launched successfully” after a git merge alone conflates all three. what happened in the 24gotop release our public eight-language draft lab change merged into the mit repository. the source ci passed and the pages deployment succeeded. the first external smoke check, however, failed : the check ran on push while the public site still served the previous version, so the new interface-language selector was absent. a later smoke check triggered by the completed pages workflow passed . that is stronger delivery evidence, not proof that the earlier failure was imaginary. the failure reflected the real state visible to the runner when it executed. we retained both run links in the deployment evidence log . fix the dependency, not the assertion the solution in pr #82 was to remove the direct push trigger from the live verification workflow. it now runs after successful completion of deploy pre-launch landing , or by explicit manual dispatch. the workflow itself needs only read access to the checkout; it cannot publish or change site settings. name: verify live draft lab release on: workflow_run: workflows: ["deploy pre-launch landing"] types: [completed] branches: [main] workflow_dispatch: permissions: contents: read jobs: verify: if: github.event_name != 'workflow_run' || github.event.workflow_run.conclusion == 'success' runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - uses: actions/checkout@v7 with: persist-credentials: false - run: bash -n scripts/check-live-draft-lab.sh - run: bash scripts/check-live-draft-lab.sh the snippet illustrates the reviewed workflow shape; consult the current workflow source for the exact maintained version. merely waiting a fixed number of seconds on every push is less reliable than waiting for the deployment event itself. a practical, read-only https smoke test our public test script downloads the canonical homepage, the experimental editor html, and its browser javascript. it restricts redirects to https, uses bounded timeouts and retries, and verifies that specific expected artifacts and safety messages are present. it does not upload content, authenticate, print response bodies or access any confidential user data. curl --fail --silent --show-error --location \ --proto '=https' --proto-redir '=https' \ --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 25 \ --output draft.html https://24go.top/draft-lab.html grep --fixed-strings 'id="uilocale"' draft.html this example checks whether the latest deployed page contains the separately controlled interface language selector. the real script also checks that the preview still protects external links and that the page honestly says it is not public article publishing. assertions should be based on stable user-facing behavior rather than brittle implementation-specific whitespace or minified line numbers. to avoid reporting a success for a mismatched release, make your check look for at least one feature unique to the revision being deployed. for more critical deployments, verify the deployed version identifier and content digest, and audit cache headers and redirects. a smoke test is not a substitute for real-browser navigation, accessibility tests or a production rollback drill. seo and ai discovery need delivery evidence too search engines and browsing agents are clients of the published site—not of your github repository. a complete sitemap only helps if its urls actually return readable html over https. verify robots.txt , sitemap.xml , rss and representative article pages separately after release. google explains that satisfying its technical requirements and having discoverable content does not guarantee indexing or ai-feature inclusion . for actual search performance you still need verified search console and bing webmaster tools properties, not estimated traffic or a site: query treated as a definitive index count. copyable checklist for your next static release review the exact commit and run project ci before merging. deploy only the expected static artifact with least-privilege github actions permissions. wait for the pages workflow success event before checking the live url. fetch canonical https pages from an external runner with safe redirects and retries. assert a release-specific feature and the site's real public-security/disclosure boundary. keep both failed and successful run links, and distinguish delivery from indexing, usage or conversion. this process is intentionally inspectable: pr #79 added the smoke , pr #82 corrected scheduling , and the live verification run records a successful externally fetched result. for the related search checklist, see publishing technical articles for people and ai search . primary sources: public github workflows, run results and code linked above. no claim of guaranteed indexing, independent user traffic or hosted production availability. explore more engineering guide · 30 october 2026 · internationalization how to localize a markdown editor without losing drafts a writer may prefer a russian interface while producing an english article, or switch to thai controls halfway through editing. a language selector must not silently translate the document, change its metadata, or mark an unchanged imported file as modified. here is a tested, source-backed approach. by 24gotop engineering · 30 october 2026 · implementation pr #81 · tests verified scope: the public 24gotop draft lab is an on-device writing prototype. it does not automatically save, upload or publish articles. its translations are first-pass and still require native-speaker and screen-reader review. the hosted 24gotop community is not launched. the trap: interface locale is not article locale a single locale variable is tempting. but there are two different decisions: the language of buttons, hints and errors; and the language of the article readers will eventually see. treating them as the same field can cause a ui preference change to rewrite exported metadata, invalidate a draft comparison or select an unintended publication language. our public editor keeps postlocale for the authored document and introduces uilocale for display strings. changing uilocale should not modify the title, body, category, source url, article locale, selection or previously reopened file baseline. a multilingual author can therefore work across languages without affecting the original writing. architecture: a fixed dictionary, not a document translation pass the translation module has eight explicit dictionaries: english, russian, thai, spanish, french, german, portuguese and chinese. every locale uses the same set of keys. missing or unexpected keys fall back to a known english string or are rejected by the lookup function. // simplified from the public implementation const ui = key => uitext(uilocale.value, key); function refreshinterface() { applyuilanguage(document, uilocale.value); preview(); message(''); } uilocale.addeventlistener('change', refreshinterface); the important part is what that handler does not do. it does not write to the draft fields, export a new file, make a network request or call a translation api. on the existing page, fixed markers such as data-ui="headline" identify interface text. text nodes are updated via textcontent , placeholders through setattribute , and html.lang is set to the current interface locale. this is much safer than accepting translated html fragments and assigning them to innerhtml . the article body is untrusted user content and remains separate from the interface dictionary. the dictionaries contain only fixed source-controlled strings, not rich text fetched from remote services. handle warnings and validation, not only button labels many incomplete localizations translate navigation but leave the most important text in english: this draft is not saved , opening a file replaces the current draft , download requested , or your selection is invalid . those messages affect irreversible choices and should be localized with the rest of the ui. in pr #81 , the eight dictionaries include 78 keys each. they cover labels, editor controls, accessibility text, error states, import confirmations and privacy notices. the english text is present directly in html so the page has meaningful static content before javascript executes. this is a local application feature, not eight translated search landing pages. preserve the file baseline during a language switch the editor supports a workflow in which a writer downloads an .md file and later reopens that exact exported file. it tracks the reopened file in a memory-only baseline. the warning before leaving depends on whether the current article actually differs from that baseline, not whether a user changed the interface labels. // conceptual invariant checked by the tests const before = { title, body, locale, category, source }; changeinterfacelanguage('ru'); assert.deepequal(currentdraft(), before); assert.equal(hasunexportedchanges(currentdraft(), baseline), false); the actual browser-simulation test reopens a locally exported markdown file, changes the interface from english to russian, and checks that every author field is unchanged. it then edits the body, confirms the unsaved-change guard becomes active, switches to chinese, and checks that the guard remains active. this catches a class of data-loss bugs that dictionary-completeness tests alone cannot detect. what about accessibility and seo? the interface-language selector has an explicit label and uses native select keyboard behavior. the page's lang attribute changes with the interface so assistive technology has an appropriate language hint. accessible labels and placeholders use the same translation keys as visible controls. we have automated assertions for those contracts; we have not measured comprehension with native speakers or tested every device/screen reader. from an seo perspective, do not create eight duplicate urls merely because a javascript control can switch the ui. genuine locale-specific articles need unique, translated visible content, correct language urls and self-consistent canonical/hreflang signals. this engineering note is an english original and declares lang="en" ; the local editor itself remains noindex because it is a prototype, not a public document to rank. reproduce the evidence inspect pr #81 and its changes to the dictionary, static html and on-device editor. run npm test after cloning the public mit repository (node.js 22 or newer). review dictionary completeness and the import-preservation test . open the live draft lab . draft a short technical explanation in english, change interface language to russian or thai, export the file, and confirm its content-language metadata still matches your selection. check the post-deployment https smoke evidence . it shows the files were served; it does not prove native-language quality. practical checklist for any multilingual editor model ui language and document language separately. keep the translation surface fixed, source-controlled and reviewable; use safe text/attribute insertion. translate destructive confirmations, status and accessibility text as well as headings. test both unchanged and dirty drafts through multiple language switches. use real bilingual readers and assistive-technology users to validate wording and navigation before launch. related reading: why we built a draft lab before public writes , how our markdown preview handles untrusted content , and all engineering notes . primary evidence: merged public pr #81 , ci source tests and post-pages live https check . no invented users, search rankings or published community articles. try the browser-only multilingual editor ↗

engineering note · 29 october 2026 · javascript & api security prevent api key leaks in javascript sdks: why https alone is not enough a developer client can support remote read requests and still carry a dangerous local-only write token. if the same client blindly attaches that token to any configured base url, a perfectly valid https request can deliver the credential to the wrong server. we found and closed this boundary in the open-source 24gotop javascript sdk prototype. 24gotop engineering · merged fix pr #56 · actual sdk implementation · negative security tests scope: this article describes a local developer prototype and its reviewed source tests. the 24gotop hosted publishing platform, verified production sessions and remote write api are not launched. no real api keys, customer data or private backend modules appear here. the failure mode: an innocent-looking remote url imagine a development sdk that defaults to http://127.0.0.1:3000 and accepts an apikey for a temporary publishing demo. the sdk also accepts a customizable baseurl , because developers may eventually query a remote read-only api. an accidental configuration change to https://some-service.example must not cause a demo publishing token to travel to that address. https authenticates the tls endpoint and encrypts transport. it does not establish that the endpoint is authorized to receive a particular credential. the question is not simply “is this url secure?” but “is this the intended recipient of this specific token?” in the 24gotop prototype, topclient.listposts() , getpost() and health() are read operations. publishpost() is different: it attaches a bearer token for a local json demo. before the fix, a user-configured https remote origin was an unsafe destination for this local credential. the first rule: validate the base url structurally the constructor parses the configured url with the standard javascript url class. it refuses non-http(s) schemes, embedded usernames/passwords, query strings, fragments and non-root paths. this removes several ambiguous or misleading input forms, but it does not by itself establish that a remote server is an approved destination for the write token. const parsed = new url(baseurl); if (!['http:', 'https:'].includes(parsed.protocol) || parsed.username || parsed.password || parsed.search || parsed.hash || parsed.pathname !== '/') { throw new typeerror('invalid api base url'); } compare parsed hostnames, not strings such as baseurl.startswith('http://127.0.0.1') . the lookalike domain 127.0.0.1.evil.example begins with those characters but is not the loopback address. similarly, a hostname containing “localhost” is not necessarily localhost . keep a local development token local for this prototype, we explicitly allow the development write credential only when the parsed destination hostname is one of three loopback names: localhost , 127.0.0.1 or ipv6 loopback [::1] . every other hostname fails before any fetch operation can run. const hostname = new url(this.baseurl).hostname; const loopback = ['localhost', '127.0.0.1', '[::1]']; if (!loopback.includes(hostname)) { throw new topclienterror( 'refusing to send a local development publishing key' ); } this guard belongs directly in publishpost() , not merely in a readme warning. it allows remote read-only experiments without sending the token, while protecting the operation that would attach authorization: bearer ... . there are additional layers: the sdk sets redirect: 'error' for requests so a fetch implementation does not silently follow a redirect to another origin. the local demo server separately restricts write requests to a verified loopback socket and validated host/origin requirements. each protects a different part of the boundary; none should be replaced by a convenient shared secret in production. reproduce the rejection without making a network request the easiest test is not to send a fake token to a remote test server. inject a fetch implementation that counts invocations, then assert the remote write is rejected before it is called. import assert from 'node:assert/strict'; import { topclient } from './packages/sdk/index.mjs'; let calls = 0; const client = new topclient({ baseurl: 'https://api.example.org', apikey: 'local_test_value_only', fetchimpl: async () => { calls += 1; throw error('should never be called'); } }); assert.throws( () => client.publishpost({ title: 'example' }), /refusing to send/ ); assert.equal(calls, 0); this uses an artificial value, not an active credential. the actual sdk test suite also rejects remote http and https origins, private lan addresses and lookalike hostnames, while confirming that unauthenticated remote reads and legitimate local publishing calls still behave according to their intended contracts. to reproduce the public source tests, clone the repository and use node.js 22 or newer: git clone https://github.com/rf24kja/24go.top.git cd 24go.top npm test these assertions verify a source-level recipient guard and the injected fetch boundary. they do not certify the underlying operating system's dns configuration, a future reverse proxy, or a production authorization scheme. four additional things an sdk security review should ask who owns the key? a shared local development token is not a production account identity. browser-visible credentials, user-owned api keys and server-held secrets have different storage and delegation rules. can redirection change the recipient? redirect following can move a request beyond an initially approved origin. require a deliberate policy and tests for redirect behavior, not an accidental default. what happens on cancellation? a pre-aborted operation should not issue a request. error messages should not echo arbitrary abort reasons that might contain sensitive values. the sdk tests these cases separately. does the server independently enforce scope? a client guard can be bypassed by a custom script or another sdk. the receiving api must authenticate and authorize the caller independently; local demo checks cannot replace user-specific production auth. what we changed, and what remains unfinished the relevant fix is publicly reviewable in pr #56 . it prevents the 24gotop sdk's publishpost() path from transmitting its local development key to remote hosts and preserves read-only requests without the publishing token. github ci and targeted node tests passed for that change. we deliberately have not presented this as a complete production sdk. real 24gotop publication still requires verified user sessions, scoped grants, database row ownership, moderation, an audit trail and independently tested backup recovery. a safe local client check does not make unreviewed public writes acceptable. related technical lessons for other security boundaries behind developer tooling, read our postgresql insert/returning privilege case study and safe markdown preview note . to see how we expect public articles to be discovered without overstating search results, read the search and ai discovery checklist . evidence: merged public pr , sdk code , unit tests and node.js url documentation . no production endpoint or external adoption is claimed. browse all engineering notes ↗

engineering note · 29 october 2026 · search & ai discovery publishing technical articles for people and ai search: a practical discovery checklist a technical project can have useful code and strong ideas yet remain invisible to search. discoverability begins with public pages that actually answer questions, stable urls, and an honest inventory of what exists. here is the approach we are implementing for 24gotop during pre-launch. 24gotop engineering · public source repository · google sitemap guidance · openai crawler guidance current scope: these engineering notes are publicly committed static files. the future hosted platform for user-submitted articles, verified ai-agent authors, comments and moderation is not launched. this article does not claim google indexing, chatgpt citations, traffic or search rankings. 1. write an answer, not a landing-page slogan a crawler can retrieve a page, but a reader still needs a reason to stay. for a developer-oriented article we start with a concrete question, describe a failure mode, show a reproducible example, and distinguish tested results from proposed changes. a generic “ai-powered community coming soon” paragraph provides little useful evidence. for example, our postgresql insert versus returning note demonstrates a specific permission distinction using a short sql example and a link to the official postgresql reference. our markdown preview security note links to a public implementation pr and tests. both remain useful even if the eventual hosted service changes. technical credibility is not a quantity target. a citation should point to an actual standard, original implementation or observed test. we do not generate fictional benchmarks, contributors, customer quotes or scraped duplicates merely to increase page count. 2. use one stable canonical url for each document links are how people, documentation tools and search engines identify a document. pick a stable hostname and page path, return readable html at that address, then use a canonical hint consistently. for this project the owner-selected domain is https://24go.top . a technical article can carry: <title>a clear technical problem — 24gotop</title> <meta name="description" content="what the article explains."> <link rel="canonical" href="https://24go.top/engineering/example.html"> a canonical tag is a signal, not a redirect. the server must actually serve that url over https. if both www and apex variants work, they should agree about the preferred address; verification requires checking real dns, redirects and http responses, not just reviewing a repository. 3. make an accurate, limited sitemap a root-level /sitemap.xml can enumerate the public pages we would like crawled. only list genuine canonical urls that are intended for indexing: the homepage, documentation index and articles. do not include private drafts, admin urls, unlaunched api endpoints, placeholder author profiles or experimental screens marked noindex . <?xml version="1.0" encoding="utf-8"?> <urlset xmlns="http://www.sitemaps.org/schemas/sitemap/0.9"> <url><loc>https://24go.top/engineering/</loc></url> </urlset> publish /robots.txt with a full sitemap: url and permit search crawlers to fetch intended pages. google's official sitemap documentation recommends absolute urls and consistently accurate modification dates; it explicitly says sitemap submission is not a guarantee of indexing. we therefore omit speculative lastmod dates, and never advertise priority as a ranking boost. 4. separate ai search visibility from model training “ai crawler” is not a single role. openai documents oai-searchbot for search visibility and gptbot for potential model-training collection, with independent choices in robots rules. chatgpt-user relates to user-triggered browsing, not general discovery. our initial public engineering content is available under an ordinary permissive crawler policy, but this does not mean an ai assistant will recommend us, quote us or rank us first. for the distinction and current crawler names, consult openai's crawler documentation . a host-level firewall or bot challenge can still prevent access even if robots.txt says allow: / . verify actual http access independently. 5. offer rss and meaningful html navigation a static html article with a descriptive heading, paragraphs, code samples and links can be read without running javascript. a small engineering index that links to each article makes the collection navigable. the engineering rss feed lists the same published notes for subscribers and tools that support rss; it contains publication dates and canonical links, not copies of private drafts. rss is a useful syndication format, not an indexing shortcut. we maintain one original url per article and link back to it from any permitted discussion or announcement. we do not mass-post backlinks to unrelated projects, manufacture citations or imply external endorsement. 6. verify discovery with evidence, then improve content check that the exact canonical page, robots.txt , sitemap and feed return readable responses from an external network, with valid https and no bot challenges. use google search console to verify domain ownership, submit the sitemap and inspect individual canonical pages. the url inspection status is more reliable than estimating indexing from a single site: search. use bing webmaster tools to monitor the other major search index. keep sitemap diagnostics and actual indexed-page counts separate from impressions and clicks. publish the next source-backed article when it teaches a reproducible lesson. compare real search queries, voluntary reader feedback and source contributions—not generated traffic or synthetic views. search engines may take days or weeks to crawl and index a new site, or they may decline to index a page. the honest success measure is a growing set of useful, verifiable documents that real readers can locate and cite, with progress tracked in search tools. what this means for 24gotop we can publish editorial engineering notes now because they are static files reviewed in public github. the hosted community is a different trust boundary: user identity, article ownership, content moderation, safe rendering and durable storage must be verified before accepting public submissions. until then, draft lab is an optional local writing experiment, not a hosted publishing account. read the engineering article archive , examine the public change log , or discuss a specific improvement through github issues . we welcome concrete corrections and independently reproducible results. references: google search central (sitemaps) , google url inspection , openai web crawlers , and 24gotop public repository . no unverified seo results claimed. browse the engineering notes ↗

engineering note · 26 october 2026 · postgresql security insert succeeds, returning fails: a least-privilege lesson a database test can fail for the right reason. when we exercised a tightly scoped insert-only role in disposable postgresql 17 ci, a convenient returning clause requested a permission the role was deliberately designed not to have. 24gotop engineering · official postgresql 17 insert reference · public security test plan #38 scope: this is a general reproducible postgresql permission lesson, inspired by a disposable ci test while designing a private, unreleased article-storage candidate. it is not evidence that 24gotop public article publishing or moderator identity checks are live. no private database sql, credentials or provider records are published here. one sql statement, two different privileges postgresql supports grants scoped to particular columns. if a role may insert an article body but must not read back other database rows, blanket grant insert, select on table is unnecessarily powerful. the difference becomes visible in an intentionally simplified example. assume a dedicated, unprivileged role has only the column grant shown below and no general read permission: grant insert (body) on example_notes to example_writer; -- write-only attempt: insert into example_notes (body) values ('a test note'); -- different access requirement: insert into example_notes (body) values ('another note') returning id; the second statement asks postgresql to return id from the affected row. that requires select permission on the referenced column in addition to the relevant insert permission. depending on row-level security configuration, a select policy may also be necessary. postgresql's insert documentation explicitly distinguishes these permissions. the tempting fix is often the wrong fix granting broad select merely to make a test assertion pass would change the application's security model. the role is meant to write, not inspect the table. a test demanding more authority than the feature requires is a test-design problem, not necessarily an application defect. in our disposable test, we removed returning and checked the insert command's row count. an independent, privileged ci fixture then inspected the saved row and compared it with the intended immutable source. we did not give the write-only role the ability to read the published-body table. that separation does not make a role magically secure. it still requires role membership checks, a non-bypassable rls policy, constraints, a controlled connection, and realistic failure tests. test effective privileges, not just grants that look right another useful postgresql distinction: table-wide insert and per-column insert rights are not interchangeable in catalog probes. a column-limited role may have permission to write body without passing a table-wide privilege check. select has_table_privilege( 'example_writer', 'example_notes', 'insert'); select has_column_privilege( 'example_writer', 'example_notes', 'body', 'insert'); tests should check the effective permission needed by the sql statement, explicitly assert that forbidden columns remain inaccessible, and try negative operations as a non-superuser. in addition, rls with force row level security is valuable defense in depth but does not replace grants or identity verification. a practical review checklist write down whether the runtime role is supposed to read, create, update or delete each field. check effective table- and column-level privileges; include prohibited operations and role membership. exercise real sql as an isolated non-superuser, including insert ... returning and duplicate-key failures where relevant. when a test fails, inspect the exact denied privilege before expanding production grants. keep privileged verification fixtures and untrusted runtime requests separate; neither a dba simulation nor a mocked jwt proves real user authorization. do not expose a public article api until moderator identity, atomic state transitions, safe rendering, takedowns and backups have been validated end to end. try the public project and review the assumptions the 24gotop open-source repository contains a local, early-stage publishing prototype, an experimental sdk and a browser-only draft lab. its ci and docs are reviewable, but it is not a launched community with public user publishing or comment threads . we welcome precise corrections and reproducible cases in security test plan #38 . a valuable follow-up would be a small public test showing how column-level grants, an rls select policy and an insert returning clause interact without ever granting broad table read. a failed permission check can be the proof that your security boundary is working. references: postgresql 17 insert — required privileges , submit for review is not publish and the 24gotop roadmap . static source publication does not establish that the article is reachable on the live domain; deployment is verified separately. suggest a security regression test ↗

engineering note · 26 october 2026 · publishing security submit for review is not publish in a technical knowledge community, the most dangerous shortcut may be treating a successfully submitted article as a successfully published one. we are separating those states before inviting people to trust the platform with their work. 24gotop engineering · public security test plan #38 · draft lab author pilot #29 · oss/hosted-core boundary release status: 24gotop is not a live community publishing service. the public repository contains an mit-licensed local prototype and a browser-only draft lab. private staging work on author-owned drafts and review intake is not deployed publicly; real two-user auth/jwt verification, moderator mfa/identity binding, full publication transactions, and backup/restore are still open gates. what can go wrong between save and publish? consider two people editing separate posts. an api accepts a json body with an author id, and a queue consumer copies it into a moderation table. the queue reports success, but the author id was never checked against a signed session. a subsequent moderation decision changes an internal status without creating a durable public article. the interface might report "published" even though nothing can be read at a stable url. these are not hypothetical capabilities we are claiming to have discovered in other products; they are failure cases we want our own project to reject. an author deserves more than a green http status code. model the lifecycle as distinct trust boundaries draft ownership: the server validates a current identity and proves that the user owns the specific draft. a client-supplied author label is not sufficient. immutable submission: submitting version n must preserve the exact reviewed title, locale, source and full body even if the author later edits version n+1 . idempotent intake: retries or two concurrent workers must not create two moderator tasks for the same submission. a failed database step must roll back its dependent changes. moderator authorization: only a verified, current, appropriately privileged moderator may approve or reject; their identity must be bound to the database decision and its audit record. atomic public release: approved content, its source submission status, a durable public body/permalink and moderation audit must agree in one transaction. a queue status alone is not a public article. reader safety: article text is untrusted. rendering, links, localization and embedded code need a reviewed policy before the url is safe for readers. a small example: why a retry key matters suppose the same review task is delivered twice following a network timeout. if each attempt generates a new moderation post id, one author may receive two conflicting decisions. our proposed invariant is a one-to-one mapping from an immutable submission_id to a single moderation item, protected by database uniqueness and a single transactional operation. submission a, version 3 → stable review identity a → at most one moderator intake record → authenticated decision + audit → one durable public revision (not implemented) a second worker should return the existing intake identity instead of silently duplicating it. if inserting the mapping fails, any associated moderator-queue insert should roll back as well. these behaviors are meaningful only when tested under actual concurrent transactions, not just mocked http responses. source-level tests for private intake proposals have been exercised in disposable postgresql 17 ci. this is evidence of the isolated sql design, not evidence that any consumer is running, real accounts were used, or production publishing works. what is publicly reproducible today? the public 24gotop repository offers an independently testable local node.js prototype, an experimental javascript sdk and a browser-only writing interface. the draft lab origin story explains why we did not connect an unfinished identity system to public writes; our markdown preview security note shows one safe way to display article-like content without executing the author's html. git clone https://github.com/rf24kja/24go.top.git cd 24go.top npm run check npm test npm run dev the repository's read-only sdk example can be run separately with npm run demo:read . an empty local feed is expected; it is not a claim of successful real-user onboarding. what we will not claim yet no announced "launched" service, public writer accounts, uploaded articles, functional comments or permanent user-facing article urls. no signed, live two-user cross-account proof merely from sql tests that simulate claims. no production moderation security assurance while actor binding and staff mfa remain unverified. no public read permission to internal staging schemas, admin tables or source submissions. no adoption numbers, fabricated testimonials, artificial stars or auto-generated community comments. see the public cross-user and race-condition test plan for specific security questions. the official founder-led hosted core is developed separately; public mit-covered code retains its existing license and independent fork rights. three focused requests for feedback we are looking for engineers who can help us answer concrete questions: should a revised article require a brand-new moderation decision? what rejection/audit information should an author see without exposing moderator identity? and what is the simplest multilingual permalink strategy that preserves attribution and correct canonical urls? join the existing security issue for reproducible security test cases, or the voluntary draft lab pilot to test writing ux. comments should describe actual observations or proposed acceptance criteria—not promotional replies or synthetic feedback. trustworthy publishing is not the speed of a button. it is the guarantee that a draft, a reviewer decision and a public page all mean what their labels say. verified public sources: project status , roadmap , test plan . private source-level work is distinguished from live system evidence. page availability on the website must be checked independently after deployment. contribute a reproducible test case ↗

engineering note · 26 october 2026 · security & ux preview markdown without executing author html a technical writing interface should display code, headings and lists clearly. but the article being typed is untrusted input. this is how we added a deliberately limited markdown preview to the 24gotop draft lab without interpreting arbitrary html. 24gotop engineering · implementation pr #40 · regression tests scope: this is a static, browser-only experiment. it cannot register users, publish to the network, or create permanent article urls. a green unit-test suite is not an external security certification. why even a preview deserves a threat model draft lab originally inserted the article body as plain text. that kept hostile markup inert, but it made writing code-oriented articles harder to review. the naive alternative—taking user-controlled markdown, treating it as html and assigning it to innerhtml —could turn a preview into an injection surface. consider an example article about unsafe image handlers. the author may intentionally type markup resembling an html image tag with an event handler, or a fenced code sample that contains script tags. those bytes are valid documentation . they should neither disappear nor become executable ui. our scope was therefore narrower than “implement all markdown.” we aimed to visually distinguish the blocks authors use most, while preserving the original text for export and avoiding new network or persistence paths. the implementation: explicit tags, literal content in pr #40 , the new preview module separates two operations. first, a small parser recognizes headings, paragraphs, lists, block quotes, horizontal rules and fenced code. second, a renderer creates only a fixed set of ordinary dom elements and assigns author-controlled strings through textcontent . const paragraph = document.createelement('p'); paragraph.textcontent = authortext; container.replacechildren(paragraph); for a fenced block, the renderer creates pre and code elements, then assigns the code sample as text. for headings, it uses lower-level headings beneath the article title to avoid breaking the page's heading hierarchy. a small amount of css keeps code blocks scrollable within mobile layouts. at the time of pr #40, the renderer did not create interactive markdown links: no markdown-provided tag, attribute, url or event handler was used. that baseline was intentionally narrower than full commonmark. update, 30 october 2026: pr #78 subsequently introduced a bounded http(s) citation-link syntax with a separate url validator and fixed dom-only anchor construction. arbitrary raw html, image embeds, scripts and unsupported markdown are still inert. read the later security analysis for the new trust boundary. what the tests actually prove the node tests exercise headings, paragraphs, ordered and unordered lists, blockquotes, code fences and unclosed fences. they also pass html-like strings into the renderer and assert that the created node types are restricted and the suspicious markup remains in textcontent . we retained the earlier draft lab import/export format: a writer can download a markdown file, leave the tab and reopen that file later. the preview does not silently upload, save or normalize away the body of the original article. developers can reproduce the source checks locally with node.js 22 or newer: git clone https://github.com/rf24kja/24go.top.git cd 24go.top npm run check npm test github actions succeeded on pr #40 . these are automated source-level checks. we have not yet completed independent screen-reader, real-device or public-url verification for the latest editor. trade-offs and what we deliberately did not build not a full markdown engine: inline emphasis, link rendering, nested lists, tables and syntax highlighting are not implemented. unknown syntax stays visible as text. not a production content renderer: real published articles still need a reviewed markdown pipeline, explicit content security policy, url rules, attribution and moderation. no draft durability unless the user exports: the preview runs locally. closing or refreshing the tab loses unsaved text. no measured adoption claim: unit tests do not tell us whether authors prefer this interface. that requires consenting volunteers and clear task results. review the code, not the hype we would value a review of the parser edge cases, mobile code overflow, keyboard behavior and accessible semantics. the draft lab user pilot still needs real independent participants; the staging security test plan concerns the separate authenticated publishing backend. neither is marked complete by the preview pr. which single code-oriented writing feature should we validate next: inline formatting, citations, syntax highlighting or an explicit markdown source/preview switch? bring a small reproducible case to the publishing rfc or the github discussions . evidence: merged pr #40 , change log and module readiness register . this article describes source implementation and known limitations, not a launched hosted product. try the experimental editor ↗

engineering note · 26 october 2026 · product & security why we built a draft lab before opening public writes a writing interface can be easy to prototype. a public publishing service requires trustworthy identity, ownership, moderation and data durability. we are deliberately treating those as different milestones. by 24gotop founder @rf24kja · initial ux pr #28 · markdown export pr #30 current product status: 24gotop is an early developer prototype, not an operational article community. the draft lab is a static, browser-only experiment. it does not sign users in, upload drafts, publish articles or generate public post urls. the problem we want to solve technical authors often spend their attention wrestling with publishing mechanics rather than explaining what they built. a useful knowledge platform should help a developer write a clear post, include a source, inspect how it reads, and confidently share it. for ai-generated material, it must also be clear who authorized the content and whether its author is a human or an agent. but “make publishing one click” is a dangerous requirement if implemented by bypassing identity checks or moderation. we want a short journey for the author without exposing a shared secret or letting anonymous actors modify someone else's work. what we have actually implemented the first prototype in pr #5 introduced a local node.js http api, a responsive reader, rss and an experimental javascript sdk. it is intended for local development; its shared-key json-file publishing endpoint is not appropriate for public writes. in pr #13 , we added a postgresql/supabase-oriented schema with row-level security (rls) policies and tests that run against an isolated postgresql instance. the policies distinguish public published articles from private drafts and separate agent credential hashes from normal client access. this is an important database security foundation, not proof of a complete production authentication system. pr #16 then introduced an optional read-only supabase feed adapter. it uses a publishable key for anonymous read requests and deliberately rejects publishing in that mode. again, no hosted account flow or production database write api is live. draft lab: learn from the interface without collecting data rather than connect an unfinished identity system to an internet-facing form, we made a static draft lab in pr #28 . a visitor can choose a language and category, enter a title and article body, optionally cite a source, and inspect a plain-text preview. the preview uses safe text insertion, not execution of whatever html happens to appear in the article. the first version allowed copying a completed draft, but that had an obvious usability weakness: clipboard permissions can fail, and refreshing the tab discards the text. in pr #30 we added an explicit local markdown download and a warning before clearing nonempty text. the user chooses when to export; we did not silently add browser persistence or cloud autosave. what the current demo deliberately does not do: send your words to a backend, create an account, track you with analytics, render arbitrary markdown as executable html, or claim the draft is published. a downloaded .md file is saved by your own browser on your device. try the developer interfaces yourself you can review the public mit-licensed source, run the local development api with node.js 22+, and exercise the no-key sdk read demo. these are two separate terminals inside the cloned repository: git clone https://github.com/rf24kja/24go.top.git cd 24go.top npm run check npm test npm run dev then, in another terminal: npm run demo:read on a clean local installation, an empty feed is expected. this is not a hosted api launch, nor does the sdk require an ai provider account. see the exact sdk quickstart for troubleshooting. what still blocks safe public publishing verified human identity: validate actual signed account sessions, expiration and ownership rather than trusting a client-supplied author label. scoped ai agent credentials: agents must be attributable to owners, have limited permissions and never silently impersonate community members. transactional persistence and tested rls: authenticated writes, migration management, recovery and backup/restore exercises must work together. moderation and abuse controls: rate limiting, reports, spam checks and auditable publication state transitions are release gates, not optional polish. author experience: accessible input, durable drafts, clear preview, source attribution and reliable share urls need validation with real authors. these are tracked in issue #2 and related engineering tasks. the official service is founder-led; a future privately hosted product core remains subject to a separate licensing decision. the existing public code retains its mit permissions. we need evidence, not invented traction the next useful result is not a vanity metric. it is a few voluntary authors trying the writing flow and showing us exactly where they hesitate. the draft lab usability pilot asks real people to write, preview and export a short technical article, then tell us if the “nothing is published” message was clear. we are also looking for focused review of the public sdk, translation quality, accessibility and the database security model. if you have a concrete integration idea, a reproducible bug or a safety concern, join the github discussions or open an appropriately scoped issue. our goal is not to be the loudest new community. it is to make publishing useful technical knowledge simpler without trading away trust. engineering evidence: changelog , decision log , security gates . this article describes verifiable source-code milestones, not confirmed product adoption, grants or a live publishing backend. try the browser-only draft lab ↗
